How to remove C2PA / Content Credentials from an image

Images made or edited with AI tools often carry a hidden, signed record of how they were created. Here is what it is, how to check for it and how to remove it.

Updated 2026-11-07 · 4 min read

Open IA Cleaner

What is C2PA?

C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) is an open standard for attaching a provenance record to a file. Adobe calls it Content Credentials. The record — called a manifest — is cryptographically signed and can say which app created the image, whether AI was used and what edits were made.

Images exported by tools such as ChatGPT / DALL·E, Adobe Firefly or Microsoft Designer, and some cameras and phones, can include a C2PA manifest. Some platforms read it to show an “AI info” or “Made with AI” label.

Where is it stored?

  • JPEG: inside APP11 segments (JUMBF boxes).
  • PNG: in a caBX chunk.
  • WebP: in a dedicated RIFF chunk.

It often travels together with XMP metadata that includes the IPTC field DigitalSourceType with values like trainedAlgorithmicMedia — another common “AI-generated” marker.

How to check if an image has Content Credentials

  1. Upload it to the official verifier at contentcredentials.org/verify, or
  2. Drop it into IA Cleaner: it lists every metadata block it finds and flags AI-related ones before removing them.

How to remove C2PA with IA Cleaner (step by step)

  1. Open IA Cleaner → Images & documents.
  2. Drag your JPG, PNG or WebP onto the drop zone (you can add several at once).
  3. Check the report: blocks such as JUMBF / C2PA Content Credentials (APP11) or XMP are listed and marked AI.
  4. Click Download. The image is cleaned losslessly — only metadata is removed, pixels stay untouched.

Verify the result by running the cleaned file through the verifier again: it should report that no Content Credentials were found.

Other ways

  • ExifTool (command line): exiftool -all= image.jpg removes EXIF, XMP and IPTC. Check its documentation for C2PA/JUMBF support in your version.
  • Screenshot or re-export: works, but recompresses the image and loses quality.

What removing C2PA does not do

Some AI images also carry invisible watermarks woven into the pixels themselves (for example Google’s SynthID). These are not metadata, so no metadata tool can remove them. And if a platform, publication or law requires you to disclose AI use, removing metadata doesn’t change that obligation.
